title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to evaluate whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used gpt‑5‑mini under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimated paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator‑detectable failures were absent on this curated bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the preregistered design, deterministic accounting that establishes single shared initial generation per task, the prominent reproducibility gap for the Mininet holdout selection seed, and artifact‑grounded interpretation and operational recommendations.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models promises operational productivity but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore recommends grounding LLMs with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR). However, the practical, workload‑conditional value of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures, (ii) validator coverage fidelity, and (iii) repair budget and prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Contributions: (1) a sealed preregistered paired experiment (n=200) isolating the marginal effect of invoking a validator+repair on identical generator outputs under shared_initial semantics; (2) complete deterministic accounting showing one shared generation per task and the observed degenerate paired outcome (no validator failures); (3) artifact‑grounded discussion of design tradeoffs, a documented reproducibility gap affecting the Mininet holdout, and concrete recommendations for future confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies show LLMs produce factual errors and are sensitive to prompt design and sampling; mitigation proposals include retrieval grounding, deterministic validators (Batfish‑style), and repair loops. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation but rarely provide instrumented, preregistered failure‑rate measurements under controlled causal contrasts. Red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness studies document that tool descriptions and agentic tool use can alter safety outcomes. Our study builds on this literature by providing an externally auditable, preregistered paired measurement that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic repair (not the unconditional effect of multi‑sample or ensemble generation). Representative prior sources include NetConfEval (W4399629579), intent→configuration prototypes and surveys (W4403635865, W4400072049), and studies of LLM hallucination and prompt sensitivity (W4399803256, W4402860127).
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The confirmatory plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and at most one automated repair attempt per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline tested with an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals used bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Task bank and validators. The task bank contained 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge). The primary checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and provides structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Adapter and sampling semantics. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate that was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This enforcement yields deterministic accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200), ensuring the paired contrast isolates the marginal effect of validating and (if required) repairing the identical generator output. Practical note on temperature and determinism: although model_configuration metadata records the model request with temperature unset, determinism in this run was achieved by adapter‑enforced shared_initial semantics and accounting that prevented independent resampling across conditions. The deterministic_reconciliation artifacts document single shared invocations per task and zero failed model calls, establishing effective deterministic treatment despite temperature being unspecified in the recorded model configuration. Reproducibility gap for Mininet holdout. The Mininet 10% holdout executed as preregistered and produced zero validator–emulator disagreements on the sampled 20 tasks; however, the explicit randomized selection seed that identifies which tasks comprised the 10% holdout is not present in the labeled artifacts. This missing seed prevents exact bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the holdout selection and therefore limits deterministic reproducibility of the Mininet disagreement check. Handling and analysis. Pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure issues would have been excluded per preregistration; any validator–emulator disagreement would have been conservatively excluded from the primary analysis. The primary exact McNemar test and bootstrap CI follow the preregistered analysis plan.
sections.results: Execution completed all planned episodes and pairs. Accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), maximum_model_calls = 400, repair_calls_used = 0. Validator outcomes: every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator—baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Under this contingency the estimated paired difference = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test: p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because the preregistered target was a ≥50% relative reduction from an assumed baseline unsafe incidence (≈30%), the absence of baseline validator failures in this sample means the primary confirmatory hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. Secondary estimands—average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, and model‑call cost per successful repair—are empty because no repair attempts occurred. The preregistered Mininet holdout check (20 tasks) reported zero validator–emulator disagreements in the contamination summary; interpret this result conditional on the documented missing holdout selection seed.
sections.discussion: Conditional interpretation. The observed null (no validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded outcome: under the chosen generator/prompt policy and the shared_initial deterministic design the LLM produced validator‑passing candidates for every task. This is not evidence that repair is intrinsically useless; rather it shows that the marginal benefit of an automated single‑attempt repair is workload dependent and vanishes when baseline validator‑detectable failures are absent. Methodological tradeoffs. The shared_initial paired design intentionally removes sampling variance to isolate the validator+repair effect on the same candidate; this increases internal control but prevents measuring unconditional failure prevalence that would arise under independent per‑condition sampling or nonzero temperature. For operational risk estimation, alternative designs that permit multi‑sample draws per condition and larger repair budgets are more informative. Validator coverage and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators encode a defined oracle; the Mininet holdout aims to detect validator blind spots. The zero disagreements in the 10% holdout indicate no detected blind spots in that sample, but the missing holdout seed limits deterministic reproducibility of that corroboration. Practical recommendations. Before investing in automated repair, practitioners should (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence under their intended generation policy, (2) evaluate validator completeness with larger emulation or testbed checks (and record holdout seeds for reproducibility), and (3) choose repair budgets and sampling strategies (multi‑sample, ensemble) appropriate to baseline failure rates. Statistical note on bootstrapping in degenerate cases. When discordant counts are zero the paired distribution is degenerate; bootstrapped percentile CIs here reflect that degeneracy (zero width CI), but such intervals convey limited inferential content about potential effects under alternative sampling regimes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic validator. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), giving an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent on this curated bank. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that automated repair’s marginal value depends on workload failure prevalence and validator coverage. Future confirmatory studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity and emulation checks (with explicit holdout seeds), evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore larger or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested; outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
